name: Fever in a baby under 6 months
summary: A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher needs to be seen by a doctor straight away, even if they seem otherwise well. Young babies can become seriously ill quickly.
redFlags: A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue (on darker skin, check the palms, soles and inside the lips)
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry that is not like their normal cry
Difficulty breathing, grunting, very fast breathing, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
A seizure (fit), or a bulging soft spot on the head
urgentFlags: A temperature of 39C (102.2F) or higher in a baby aged 3 to 6 months
Not feeding, or feeding much less than usual
Fewer wet nappies, or no wet nappy for 8 hours or more
Vomiting repeatedly, or green vomit
Fever with a rash, or a fever that lasts 5 days or more
You feel something is seriously wrong

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds and other viruses are the most common cause, but young babies need checking to rule out serious infection.

commonCauses.title: Vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: A mild temperature after vaccinations is common; some vaccines can cause fever within 48 hours.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infections
commonCauses.detail: Urine infections, chest infections, sepsis or meningitis are less common but serious in young babies.

selfCare: Get medical help straight away if your baby is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38C or higher
Keep offering breast or formula milk little and often
Dress your baby in light clothing; do not wrap them up or bundle them in blankets
Paracetamol can be given from 2 months and ibuprofen from 3 months (if over 5kg), following the pack instructions; check with a pharmacist or doctor first for young babies
Check on your baby regularly during the night
avoid: Sponging your baby with cold water or giving cold baths
Giving aspirin to a baby or child under 16
Giving paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time, unless a doctor advises it
Waiting to see if a fever in a baby under 3 months settles
seeDoctorIf: Your baby seems unwell or not their usual self, even without a high temperature
Your baby has had a temperature after vaccination for more than 48 hours
You are worried about your baby

name: Fever in a child
summary: A high temperature is very common in children and is usually caused by a viral infection that the body can fight off. Watch how your child is behaving as well as the number on the thermometer.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue (on darker skin, check the palms, soles and inside the lips)
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
Difficulty breathing, grunting, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A stiff neck or pain looking at bright lights
A seizure (fit) for the first time
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
urgentFlags: A temperature that lasts 5 days or more
Not drinking, or signs of dehydration such as a dry mouth, no tears or peeing much less
Your child is getting worse, or you are worried
A fever with ear pain, pain when peeing, or a sore throat with white spots
A fever in a child with a long-term condition or weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu and other viruses are the most common cause and get better on their own.

commonCauses.title: Ear, throat or urine infections
commonCauses.detail: Some may need antibiotics.

commonCauses.title: Childhood illnesses
commonCauses.detail: Chickenpox, hand, foot and mouth disease, and scarlet fever often start with a fever.

commonCauses.title: Vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: A mild temperature after vaccines is common and usually settles within 48 hours.

selfCare: Give plenty of fluids, and breast or formula milk for babies
Look out for signs of dehydration
Give food if your child wants it
Use children's paracetamol or ibuprofen if your child is distressed, following the pack instructions for their age; do not give ibuprofen if they have chickenpox
Check on your child regularly during the night and keep them off nursery or school while they have a temperature
avoid: Undressing your child completely, sponging with cold water, or over-wrapping them
Giving aspirin to anyone under 16
Giving paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time, unless a doctor advises it
seeDoctorIf: The temperature has lasted more than 3 days and your child is not improving
Your child keeps getting high temperatures
You are worried about your child

name: Baby crying non-stop
summary: All babies cry, and colic, wind and tiredness are common reasons. Crying that sounds different, or comes with a fever or your baby being unwell, needs to be checked.
redFlags: A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry that is not like their normal cry
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
Difficulty breathing, blue or grey lips, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Green vomit, or blood in their poo
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it, or a bulging soft spot on the head
urgentFlags: Crying with not feeding, or vomiting most feeds
Crying with a high temperature
Fewer wet nappies than usual
Crying that seems to come with pain, such as drawing up the legs repeatedly with paleness
A swelling in the groin or a swollen, red scrotum

commonCauses.title: Hunger, tiredness or a dirty nappy
commonCauses.detail: The most common reasons for crying.

commonCauses.title: Colic
commonCauses.detail: Long periods of crying, often in the evening, in an otherwise healthy baby; usually starts in the first few weeks and improves by 3 to 4 months.

commonCauses.title: Wind or reflux
commonCauses.detail: Discomfort during or after feeds.

commonCauses.title: Illness
commonCauses.detail: Infections, ear pain or, rarely, a twisted bowel or hernia.

selfCare: Check if your baby is hungry, tired, too hot or too cold, or needs a nappy change
Hold your baby close, rock or walk gently, and try white noise or a warm bath
Wind your baby during and after feeds
If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby safely on their back in their cot and take a few minutes to calm down
Ask your health visitor, midwife or doctor for support
avoid: Ever shaking a baby; this can cause serious brain injury
Changing formula repeatedly without advice
Unproven colic remedies, herbal teas or giving water to young babies
seeDoctorIf: Your baby cries a lot and you are struggling to cope
Your baby is not gaining weight or feeding well
Crying has not improved by 4 months
You think your baby might have reflux or a cow's milk allergy

name: Rash in a baby or child
summary: Most rashes in children are harmless and caused by viruses, heat or skin irritation. A rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, or a rash with a child who is unwell, needs urgent help.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it (on darker skin, check paler areas such as palms, soles and inside the eyelids)
A rash with a stiff neck, pain looking at bright lights, or confusion
A rash with floppiness, drowsiness, or being hard to wake
A rash with swelling of the lips, tongue or face, or difficulty breathing
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin with feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A rash with a high temperature and your child seems unwell
A rash with a sore throat, swollen glands and a red 'strawberry' tongue
A temperature for 5 days or more with red eyes, cracked lips or swollen hands and feet
Blistering, crusting or spreading rash that may be infected
Chickenpox in a baby under 4 weeks, or with a high temperature, chest pain or difficulty breathing

commonCauses.title: Viral rashes
commonCauses.detail: Blotchy rashes with a cold or fever that fade within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Chickenpox or hand, foot and mouth disease
commonCauses.detail: Itchy spots that blister, or spots on the hands, feet and in the mouth.

commonCauses.title: Eczema or heat rash
commonCauses.detail: Dry, itchy patches, or tiny red spots when overheated.

commonCauses.title: Impetigo or scarlet fever
commonCauses.detail: Crusty golden sores, or a rough, sandpaper-like rash with sore throat; may need treatment.

commonCauses.title: Meningitis or sepsis
commonCauses.detail: Rare, but the reason to do the glass test and act fast.

selfCare: Do the glass test: press the side of a clear glass firmly on the rash and see if it fades
Keep your child cool and give plenty of fluids
Use children's paracetamol for discomfort, following the pack instructions for their age
For itchy rashes, keep nails short and use plain moisturisers or calamine lotion
Keep your child off nursery or school until you know whether the rash is infectious
avoid: Ibuprofen if your child has chickenpox
Aspirin for anyone under 16
Contact with pregnant people, newborns and people with weakened immune systems if chickenpox is possible
seeDoctorIf: A rash has not cleared after a week
A rash is painful, spreading or affecting sleep
You are unsure what the rash is

sources.label: NHS: Rashes in babies and children

name: Barking cough in a child (croup)
summary: Croup is a common viral illness in young children that causes a barking cough, a hoarse voice and noisy breathing. Most cases are mild and get better within 48 hours, but some children need treatment.
redFlags: Your child is struggling to breathe, or the skin is sucking in under the ribs or at the neck
Blue, grey or very pale lips or skin
Your child is unusually drowsy, floppy, quiet or not responding
Your child is drooling, cannot swallow, or is leaning forward to breathe
Your child stops breathing for a moment
urgentFlags: A harsh, high-pitched noise when breathing in (stridor) even when calm or resting
Symptoms that are getting worse
A high temperature or your child seems very unwell
Your child is restless or agitated, or not drinking

commonCauses.title: Viral croup
commonCauses.detail: Caused by viruses such as parainfluenza; most common between 6 months and 3 years.

commonCauses.title: Spasmodic croup
commonCauses.detail: Sudden barking cough at night that can come back.

commonCauses.title: Other causes of noisy breathing
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, an inhaled object or a serious throat infection.

selfCare: Keep your child calm and sit them upright; crying can make symptoms worse
Give plenty of fluids
Use children's paracetamol or ibuprofen for a high temperature or discomfort, following the pack instructions for their age
Check on your child regularly during the night
avoid: Putting your child in a steamy room or using steam, which is not proven to help and can cause scalds
Cough medicines for young children
Smoking around your child
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not improved after 2 days
Your child keeps getting croup
You are worried about your child's breathing

name: Fast or noisy breathing in a baby
summary: Bronchiolitis is a common chest infection in babies under 2 that starts like a cold and can cause a cough, fast breathing and difficulty feeding. Most babies get better at home within 2 to 3 weeks.
redFlags: Your baby is struggling to breathe, grunting, or the skin is sucking in under the ribs
Pauses in breathing, or blue or grey lips or tongue
Your baby is floppy, unresponsive or very hard to wake
Your baby is too breathless to feed or make sounds
urgentFlags: Feeding less than half the usual amount over the last 2 or 3 feeds
No wet nappy for 12 hours or more
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher under 3 months, or 39C (102.2F) or higher at 3 to 6 months
Breathing faster than usual or getting worse
A baby born prematurely or with a heart or lung condition who has these symptoms

commonCauses.title: Bronchiolitis
commonCauses.detail: A viral chest infection, most often caused by RSV, common in winter.

commonCauses.title: Colds
commonCauses.detail: A blocked nose can make breathing sound noisy and make feeding harder.

commonCauses.title: Viral wheeze or asthma
commonCauses.detail: Older babies and toddlers can wheeze with colds.

selfCare: Offer smaller feeds more often
Saline nose drops from a pharmacy can help with a blocked nose before feeds
Keep your baby upright when they are awake to help breathing
Use paracetamol or ibuprofen only if your baby is old enough and distressed, following the pack instructions
Keep your baby away from smoke
avoid: Smoking near your baby, in the home or car
Cough medicines or decongestants for babies
Raising the cot mattress or putting your baby to sleep on their front
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms are not improving after 3 days
The cough has lasted more than 3 weeks
You are worried about your baby

name: Nappy rash
summary: Nappy rash is very common and causes red, sore patches in the nappy area. It usually clears in a few days with simple care and a barrier cream.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it, with your baby seeming unwell
Your baby is floppy, very drowsy, or has a temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher under 3 months
urgentFlags: Blisters, open sores, pus or crusting in the nappy area
A rash with a high temperature
Bright red rash with spots spreading into the skin folds that is not improving

commonCauses.title: Irritation from wee and poo
commonCauses.detail: Skin in contact with a wet or dirty nappy for too long.

commonCauses.title: Fragranced products
commonCauses.detail: Soaps, bubble bath, lotions or wipes containing alcohol or perfume.

commonCauses.title: Thrush infection
commonCauses.detail: A bright red rash with spots, often in the skin folds; may need antifungal cream.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infection
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, sores, blisters or crusts that need treatment.

selfCare: Change wet or dirty nappies as soon as possible
Clean the skin with water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free baby wipes, and pat dry
Leave the nappy off for as long as practical each day
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream at each change
Bath your baby daily, but not more than twice a day
avoid: Soap, bubble bath and lotions in the nappy area
Talcum powder
Tight nappies or clothing over the nappy area
Using steroid creams on a baby's nappy area unless a doctor advises it
seeDoctorIf: The rash has not cleared after a week of self-care
The rash keeps coming back
You think the rash may be thrush

name: Vomiting in babies and children
summary: Vomiting in children is usually caused by a stomach bug and stops within 1 to 2 days. The main risk is dehydration, especially in babies.
redFlags: Green or yellow-green vomit, or vomit with blood or that looks like coffee grounds
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
A stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, or a bulging soft spot
Severe tummy pain or a swollen, hard tummy
Signs of severe dehydration such as no wet nappies or not peeing all day, cold hands and feet, or sunken eyes
urgentFlags: A baby under 1 who will not take feeds or keeps vomiting feeds
Signs of dehydration such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth or no tears
Vomiting for more than 2 days, or with diarrhoea for more than 2 days in a child under 5
Forceful (projectile) vomiting after every feed in a baby under 2 months
Vomiting after a head injury
Vomiting in a child with diabetes

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug
commonCauses.detail: Gastroenteritis, usually with diarrhoea, is the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Posseting and reflux
commonCauses.detail: Bringing up small amounts of milk after feeds is normal in babies who are feeding and growing well.

commonCauses.title: Other infections
commonCauses.detail: Ear, throat or urine infections can make children vomit.

commonCauses.title: Pyloric stenosis or blockage
commonCauses.detail: Less common; forceful vomiting in young babies or green vomit needs urgent checking.

selfCare: Keep breast or formula feeding little and often
Give small, frequent sips of fluids; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy helps
Offer food when your child feels able
Wash hands often and keep children off nursery or school until 48 hours after the last episode
avoid: Fruit juice or fizzy drinks
Anti-sickness or anti-diarrhoea medicines for children unless a doctor prescribes them
Diluting formula milk
seeDoctorIf: Your baby keeps bringing up feeds and is not gaining weight
Vomiting keeps coming back
You are worried about your child

name: Diarrhoea in babies and children
summary: Diarrhoea in children is usually caused by a stomach bug and gets better within 5 to 7 days. Keeping them drinking is the most important thing.
redFlags: Blood in the poo with your child seeming very unwell
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
Signs of severe dehydration such as no wet nappies or not peeing all day, cold hands and feet, or sunken eyes
Severe tummy pain or a swollen tummy
Green vomit with diarrhoea
urgentFlags: Signs of dehydration such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth, no tears or a sunken soft spot on the head
Blood in the poo
A baby under 6 months with diarrhoea and a high temperature
Diarrhoea with vomiting for more than 2 days in a child under 5

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug
commonCauses.detail: Viruses such as rotavirus and norovirus are the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: From contaminated food or water.

commonCauses.title: Antibiotics
commonCauses.detail: Can upset the normal balance of gut bacteria.

commonCauses.title: Toddler's diarrhoea
commonCauses.detail: Loose poo with undigested food in a well, growing toddler; often linked to lots of juice.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance or allergy
commonCauses.detail: For example cow's milk protein allergy in babies.

selfCare: Keep breast or formula feeding; offer extra fluids little and often
Use oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy if your child is at risk of dehydration
Offer food when your child feels able
Wash hands thoroughly and keep children off nursery or school until 48 hours after the last episode
avoid: Fruit juice or fizzy drinks
Anti-diarrhoea medicines for children under 12
Swimming pools for 2 weeks after the diarrhoea stops
seeDoctorIf: Diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days
Diarrhoea keeps coming back
Your child is not gaining weight or is losing weight

name: Baby floppy, drowsy or not feeding
summary: A baby who is unusually floppy, very drowsy or not feeding can be seriously ill, even without a high temperature. Trust your instincts and get help quickly.
redFlags: Floppy, unresponsive, or very hard to wake
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
Difficulty breathing, grunting, pauses in breathing, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
A seizure (fit), or a bulging soft spot on the head
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months, or a temperature below 36C (96.8F)
urgentFlags: Feeding much less than usual or refusing feeds
Fewer wet nappies than usual, or no wet nappy for 8 hours or more
Vomiting most feeds
Yellow skin or eyes with sleepiness and poor feeding
Your baby is just not themselves and you are worried

commonCauses.title: Infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds and viruses can reduce feeding; serious infections such as sepsis or meningitis must be ruled out.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration
commonCauses.detail: From vomiting, diarrhoea or poor feeding.

commonCauses.title: Jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Newborns with jaundice can be sleepy and feed poorly.

commonCauses.title: Feeding difficulties
commonCauses.detail: Problems with latch or positioning, or a blocked nose.

selfCare: Get medical help straight away if any warning signs are present
Keep offering feeds little and often
Count wet nappies and note when your baby last fed
Ask a midwife, health visitor or doctor for feeding support
avoid: Waiting overnight to see if a floppy or very drowsy baby improves
Giving water or other drinks instead of milk to young babies
seeDoctorIf: Your baby is not gaining weight
Feeding is often difficult or painful
You are worried about your baby's feeding or sleep

name: Yellow skin in a newborn
summary: Jaundice is common in newborn babies and usually harmless, fading within 2 weeks. Some babies need checks or treatment, so tell your midwife, health visitor or doctor if you notice it.
redFlags: Your baby is floppy, very drowsy, hard to wake or not feeding
A seizure (fit), arching of the back or a high-pitched cry
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher
urgentFlags: Jaundice that starts in the first 24 hours after birth
Pale, chalky-coloured poo or dark yellow pee
Jaundice getting deeper or spreading, or your baby is sleepy and not feeding well
Jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks (3 weeks if born early)

commonCauses.title: Physiological jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Very common; the baby's liver is still developing and it usually clears within 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Breast milk jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Can last longer in breastfed babies and is usually harmless.

commonCauses.title: Blood group differences or infection
commonCauses.detail: Can cause jaundice in the first 24 hours.

commonCauses.title: Liver problems
commonCauses.detail: Rare; pale poo and dark pee need urgent checking.

selfCare: Tell your midwife, health visitor or doctor if you think your baby looks yellow
Feed your baby often, at least 8 to 12 times a day in the first days
Check the colour of your baby's poo and pee
Check for yellowing in the whites of the eyes, gums or palms, especially on darker skin
avoid: Putting your baby in direct sunlight to treat jaundice
Giving water or glucose water instead of milk
seeDoctorIf: You notice any yellowing of your baby's skin or eyes
Your baby's poo is pale or pee is dark
You are worried about how much your baby is feeding

name: Fit or seizure with a fever in a child
summary: Fits caused by a high temperature are fairly common in children aged 6 months to 5 years and are usually harmless, but a first fit always needs urgent medical assessment.
redFlags: It is your child's first fit
A fit that lasts more than 5 minutes
Your child does not wake up or is not breathing normally after the fit
Your child has another fit during the same illness
A stiff neck, a rash that does not fade with the glass test, or very drowsy after the fit
urgentFlags: A short fit in a child who has had febrile seizures before, once they have recovered
A fever that is not settling
Signs of an infection such as ear pain, vomiting or not drinking

commonCauses.title: High temperature from a viral infection
commonCauses.detail: The most common trigger, often at the start of an illness.

commonCauses.title: Other infections
commonCauses.detail: Ear, throat or urine infections; rarely meningitis.

commonCauses.title: After vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, a fever after vaccination can trigger a febrile seizure.

selfCare: Place your child on their side on a soft surface, away from anything they could hit
Stay with them and time the fit
Once the fit stops, put them in the recovery position and check their breathing
Use children's paracetamol or ibuprofen for comfort afterwards, following the pack instructions for their age
avoid: Putting anything in your child's mouth during a fit
Holding them down or trying to stop the movements
Cold baths or sponging to bring down the temperature
seeDoctorIf: Your child has had a febrile seizure and you want advice on what to do next time
Your child has fits without a fever

name: Stomach ache in a child
summary: Tummy aches are very common in children and are usually caused by constipation, wind, a stomach bug or worry. Severe or worsening pain needs to be checked.
redFlags: Severe pain that does not ease, or a hard, swollen tummy
Green vomit, or vomit with blood
Blood or redcurrant-jelly-like material in the poo with pain that comes and goes
Sudden pain in the testicles, groin or scrotum in a boy
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
urgentFlags: Pain that moves to the lower right side or is worse when walking or jumping
Pain with a high temperature
Pain when peeing or peeing more often
Pain with not drinking or signs of dehydration
Pain that keeps getting worse over several hours

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: One of the most common causes of tummy ache in children.

commonCauses.title: Stomach bugs
commonCauses.detail: With vomiting or diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Wind, colic or eating too much
commonCauses.detail: Usually mild and short-lived.

commonCauses.title: Worry or stress
commonCauses.detail: Tummy aches can happen with anxiety about school or other things.

commonCauses.title: Appendicitis or urine infection
commonCauses.detail: Less common but need treatment.

selfCare: Let your child rest and give small sips of water
Give children's paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions for their age
A warm (not hot) water bottle wrapped in a towel can help
Offer plain food when they feel like eating
avoid: Aspirin for anyone under 16
Laxatives unless a doctor has advised them
Fatty or spicy food while the pain lasts
seeDoctorIf: Tummy aches keep coming back
Your child is not growing or gaining weight
Your child has ongoing constipation or diarrhoea
Pain is linked to worry or affecting school

name: Constipation in a child
summary: Constipation is common in children and can usually be helped with more fluids, fibre and a regular toilet routine. Some children need medicine from a doctor.
redFlags: A swollen tummy with green vomit
Severe tummy pain, or a baby who is floppy and not feeding
urgentFlags: Constipation in a baby in the first few weeks of life
Blood in the poo
Constipation with a high temperature, vomiting or a very swollen tummy
Weakness in the legs or problems walking

commonCauses.title: Not enough fibre or fluid
commonCauses.detail: Very common, especially in fussy eaters.

commonCauses.title: Holding in poo
commonCauses.detail: Because of pain, fear of the toilet, or during toilet training.

commonCauses.title: Changes in routine or diet
commonCauses.detail: Starting solids, switching to cow's milk or travel.

commonCauses.title: Medical causes
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, conditions affecting the bowel, nerves or thyroid.

selfCare: Give plenty of fluids, especially water
Offer fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrains if your child is eating solids
Encourage a regular toilet routine after meals, with a footstool so their knees are higher than their hips
Praise your child for using the toilet, even if nothing happens
avoid: Giving adult laxatives or suppositories without advice
Punishing or pressuring a child over toilet use
Adding extra water to formula milk
seeDoctorIf: Constipation has not improved with diet changes after 2 weeks
Your child is soiling their pants
Your child is in pain when pooing or has a sore bottom
Your child is not growing well or losing weight

name: Limping or hip pain in a child
summary: A limp in a child is often caused by a minor injury or a short-lived inflamed hip after a virus, but a limp without a clear cause should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: A limp or refusing to walk with a high temperature and seeming very unwell
A very painful, hot, swollen joint with a high temperature
A limb that looks deformed after an injury
urgentFlags: A limp or not putting weight on a leg with no clear injury
A limp with a high temperature
A limp in a child under 3
Hip, thigh or knee pain with a limp in an older child or teenager
A limp that is getting worse

commonCauses.title: Minor injury
commonCauses.detail: Bumps, sprains or a splinter in the foot.

commonCauses.title: Irritable hip
commonCauses.detail: A short-lived hip inflammation after a virus, most common at ages 3 to 10; usually settles within 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Joint or bone infection
commonCauses.detail: Rare but serious; usually with fever and severe pain.

commonCauses.title: Hip conditions
commonCauses.detail: Perthes disease in younger children, or a slipped growth plate in teenagers, which can cause knee pain.

selfCare: Check the foot and leg for splinters, cuts or swelling
Give children's paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions for their age
Let your child rest while you arrange for them to be checked
avoid: Making your child walk through pain
Assuming a limp is a growing pain
seeDoctorIf: Your child has been diagnosed with irritable hip and is not better after 2 weeks
The limp keeps coming back
Your child has joint pain with a rash or tiredness

name: Teething
summary: Teething can make babies sore, dribbly and unsettled, usually from around 6 months. Teething does not cause a high temperature or illness.
redFlags: A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Floppy, unresponsive or very hard to wake
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
urgentFlags: A temperature of 39C (102.2F) or higher in a baby aged 3 to 6 months
Not feeding or drinking, or fewer wet nappies
Diarrhoea or vomiting, which are not caused by teething

commonCauses.title: Teeth coming through
commonCauses.detail: Red, swollen gums, drooling, chewing and being unsettled.

commonCauses.title: Other illnesses
commonCauses.detail: Fever, diarrhoea or a rash suggest an infection rather than teething.

selfCare: Give your baby a teething ring cooled in the fridge (not the freezer)
Gently rub the gums with a clean finger
From 6 months, offer healthy, sugar-free foods to chew, such as cold pieces of vegetable, and stay with them
Children's paracetamol or ibuprofen can be used from the right age if your baby is distressed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Amber teething necklaces or bracelets, which can cause choking or strangulation
Teething gels with local anaesthetic, such as benzocaine or lidocaine, for young babies unless a pharmacist advises
Frozen teething rings or sugary foods and drinks
seeDoctorIf: Your baby has symptoms of illness, such as a high temperature
No teeth have come through by 12 months
You are worried about your baby's teeth
